body_md: Round robin cycles requests evenly and works when nodes match. Keep weights for unequal boxes and rely on fast failure detection because blind rotation still hits sick hosts.
code:
let i = counter.fetch_add(1, SeqCst) % nodes.len();
forward(&nodes[i], req).await // simple cycle
hook: Round robin: fair rotation for identical backends.
output:
req -> nodes[i], i cycles 0..n-1
// even split on equal boxes; eject sick hosts fast

quiz.explain: Plain rotation assumes equal capacity and cost per request; health checks still have to eject sick hosts.
options: Identical backends with similar request costs
Requests with wildly different durations
Sessions that must always stick to one backend
Backends with very uneven hardware sizes
quiz.q: When does round robin shine?

takeaway: Use weighted rotation for uniform nodes behind health checks.
trap: Rotating blindly into a dead node without ejection.

body_md: Least connections sends traffic to the emptiest backend. It adapts to slow nodes and long requests but needs accurate counts and warmup guards for fresh hosts.
code:
let n = nodes.iter().min_by_key(|n| n.inflight())
    .expect("node"); // route to emptiest
hook: Least connections: send work where the line is shortest.
output:
req -> node with min inflight (emptiest)
// slow nodes get less; slow-start fresh hosts

quiz.explain: Live in-flight counts steer around slow, busy backends; new hosts need slow-start so they are not flooded.
options: Request costs vary, so live counts beat rotation
It guarantees each user always hits the same backend
It needs no state about backend health or load
New hosts should get a burst of traffic first
quiz.q: Why pick least connections?

takeaway: Route to the emptiest host when request costs vary widely.
trap: Flooding a just-started node that reports zero load.

body_md: Maglev hashing gives stable sticking with minimal churn on membership change. Big lookup table plus per-host permutations reassign only moved ranges so sessions survive resizes.
hook: Maglev hashing: sticky routing that survives host churn.

quiz.explain: Permutation tables remap only affected entries on change.
options: It hashes keys mod N for simple stable routing
Every LB syncs its session table with all its peers
DNS steers each client to a fixed backend IP
Even spread with minimal remap when hosts change
quiz.q: What makes Maglev good for load balancers?

takeaway: Use Maglev tables for sticky routes that survive membership shifts.
trap: Using modulo hashing and reshuffling every session on scale.

body_md: Health checks separate alive from ready to serve. Probe a cheap dependency-aware endpoint, flap-dampen failures, and eject fast while keeping a small outlier pool for recovery.
hook: Health checks: stop sending traffic to dying backends.
output:
db ok -> 200 ready (gets traffic)
db down -> 503, ejected fast, damped vs flaps

quiz.explain: Dependency-aware readiness plus damping avoids flapping traffic.
options: A TCP connect check on the service port is enough
Deep checks of every downstream on each probe
Readiness probes with flap damping, fast eject
Eject a host permanently on its first failed probe
quiz.q: What makes health checks reliable?

takeaway: Probe readiness with dependencies and dampen flapping decisions.
trap: Marking ready on TCP accept while the database is down.

body_md: Terminate TLS at the edge so backends skip handshake math. Keep certs central, enforce modern versions, and pass identity downstream with verified headers or mutual TLS inside.
hook: TLS termination: do the handshakes at the edge.

quiz.explain: The edge does the handshake math and holds certs centrally; inside traffic still needs mTLS or verified identity headers.
options: It makes inside traffic secure without any TLS
So backends can verify client certs themselves
Central certs and backends skip handshake work
It removes the need for certificates entirely
quiz.q: Why terminate TLS at the load balancer?

takeaway: Offload handshakes at the edge and propagate verified identity inward.
trap: Trusting spoofable identity headers from the open internet.

body_md: CDN cache keys must include what varies the bytes like path, query allowlist, encoding, and auth class. Normalize junk queries and version assets so hits stay high and private data never mixes.
code:
// key = METHOD + host + path + sorted(allowed query)
// vary: Accept-Encoding, Country; never mix user ids
hook: Cache keys decide your hit ratio fate.
output:
GET /feed?user=7&xjunk=1 -> key drops junk + user
// shared hits stay high; private never under a public key

quiz.explain: Minimal varying key with normalization boosts hits safely.
options: Use the full raw URL with every query param
Key only on path so all variants share a hit
Cache Set-Cookie responses for all users
Normalize queries and vary by auth class
quiz.q: How do you build safe CDN cache keys?

takeaway: Normalize cache keys and isolate private responses by identity.
trap: Caching personalized pages under a shared public key.

body_md: Token bucket allows bursts while capping average rate. Refill tokens on elapsed time and spend one per request so APIs absorb spikes without drowning backends.
code:
bucket.tokens = (bucket.tokens + elapsed * rate).min(cap);
if bucket.tokens >= 1.0 { bucket.tokens -= 1.0; allow() }
hook: Token bucket: bursts welcome, floods politely declined.
output:
tokens refill elapsed*rate (cap); >= 1.0 -> allow + deduct
// bursts to cap, average to rate

quiz.explain: Bucket depth sets burst while refill sets sustained rate.
options: When every burst must be rejected outright
Bursty APIs that need a capped average rate
When you need exact counts per calendar day
When traffic is smooth and never bursts at all
quiz.q: When is token bucket the right limiter?

takeaway: Use token buckets to allow bursts while capping average load.
trap: Setting bucket depth huge and calling it rate limiting.

body_md: Sliding window counts recent requests with smoother edges than fixed windows. Track timestamps in Redis sorted sets and expire old entries so boundary bursts cannot double-spend quota.
hook: Sliding window: count the last minute, not the calendar one.
output:
now added; entries older than window trimmed
count = members inside window (no edge doubling)

quiz.explain: Continuous windows remove fixed-boundary quota doubling.
options: It needs less memory than a fixed counter
Stops 2x bursts at the window boundary
It lets clients bank unused quota for later
It resets everyone's quota at the same time
quiz.q: Why prefer sliding window over fixed window?

takeaway: Count rolling windows to stop boundary bursts from doubling quota.
trap: Using fixed windows that allow twice the quota at edges.

body_md: Retry with capped exponential backoff plus jitter spreads stampedes. Retry only idempotent errors, cap attempts, and add hedged deadline so one slow shard cannot stall everything.
code:
let d = min(cap, base * 2_u64.pow(n)) + rand(0..250);
sleep(d).await; // jittered backoff, idempotent only
hook: Retries with jitter: rain, not a thundering herd.
output:
d = min(cap, base*2^n) + jitter(0..250ms); sleep, retry
// idempotent errors only; attempts capped

quiz.explain: Jitter desynchronizes clients while caps bound worst latency.
options: Retry immediately so the user waits less time
Retry every error, including non-idempotent POSTs
Jittered backoff, capped, idempotent calls only
Use the same fixed delay for every client
quiz.q: Safe retry recipe for flaky calls?

takeaway: Retry idempotent calls with capped jittered backoff and limits.
trap: Retrying non-idempotent payments without idempotency keys.

body_md: Circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency and fails fast. It trips after error threshold, probes with half-open traffic, and closes when success returns.
code:
if breaker.is_open() { return fallback(); }
// half-open: allow one probe, close on success
hook: Circuit breakers: fail fast today, stay alive tomorrow.
output:
open -> fallback() at once, zero doomed calls
// half-open probe closes the breaker on success

quiz.explain: Open circuits shed doomed work and let dependencies recover.
options: Only the database from slow, unindexed queries
Callers and a failing dependency from overload
Requests from failing, by retrying until success
The network from packet loss and timeouts
quiz.q: What does a circuit breaker protect?

takeaway: Trip failing calls fast and probe recovery through half-open traffic.
trap: Keeping the breaker closed during a full downstream outage.

body_md: Bulkhead isolates pools so one bad tenant cannot sink all. Split threads, connections, and queues per dependency with per-lane caps and separate timeouts.
hook: Bulkheads: one leak should not sink the whole ship.
output:
payments pool(20) full -> only payments shed
search pool(50) unaffected (blast radius contained)

quiz.explain: Per-lane caps contain blast radius across tenants.
options: One shared pool sized for peak traffic
Separate pools and caps per dependency
Longer timeouts so slow calls can finish
A global queue that orders all requests
quiz.q: How do bulkheads contain failures?

takeaway: Isolate resources per dependency with independent capacity caps.
trap: Sharing one pool across critical and best-effort traffic.

body_md: Timeout budgets cap total wait across chained calls. Set per-attempt deadlines smaller than the edge budget and propagate remaining time so deep calls cannot blow the user deadline.
code:
let left = deadline.saturating_sub(now());
call.with_timeout(left / 2).await?; // leave room
hook: Timeout budgets: deadlines must shrink as calls chain.
output:
left = deadline - now; call gets left/2
// deep chain still meets the edge budget

quiz.explain: Propagated deadlines bound tail latency across the chain.
options: Pass the remaining deadline down each hop
Every hop gets the same full edge timeout again
Inner calls get longer timeouts than outer
Retries reset the clock so each try is fresh
quiz.q: How do timeout budgets work?

takeaway: Propagate shrinking deadlines so chained calls respect edge limits.
trap: Giving every hop the full edge timeout and stacking waits.

body_md: Backpressure signals overload upstream instead of queueing forever. Bound queues, shed low-priority load with 429 plus Retry-After, and autoscale on queue depth rather than hope.
code:
if queue.len() > max { return status(429); }
// signal Retry-After, drop tail low priority
hook: Load shedding: say no fast so important work survives.
output:
len > max -> 429 + Retry-After, low priority shed
// queue depth drives autoscale

quiz.explain: Bounded queues plus explicit shedding keep latency stable.
options: Bound queues, shed low priority with 429
Grow queues so no request is ever dropped
Accept all and let timeouts sort it out
Drop requests at random across all tiers
quiz.q: Healthy response to sustained overload?

takeaway: Bound queues and shed low priority load with clear retry signals.
trap: Growing an unbounded queue until memory kills the host.

body_md: HPA scales on signals like CPU, request queue, and custom latency. Pick leading indicators, cool down flaps, and scale stateful parts separately from stateless web tiers.
hook: Autoscaling: scale on signals, not midnight panic.

quiz.explain: Leading metrics plus cooldowns scale before saturation hits.
options: Leading signals plus cooldowns, tiers separate
CPU alone, with no cooldown so it can react fast
Scale the database with the web tier together
Scale only after p99 latency already doubled
quiz.q: What makes autoscaling stable?

takeaway: Scale on leading signals with cooldowns per tier.
trap: Scaling on lagging CPU alone during queue buildup.

body_md: Readiness gates traffic while liveness triggers restarts. Fail readiness when dependencies sag, fail liveness only on deadlock, and never couple deploys to aggressive restart thresholds.
code:
async fn live() -> Status { ok() } // cheap, no deps
async fn ready() -> Status { deps_ok().await }
hook: Readiness vs liveness: ready means serve, alive means spare.
output:
live(): 200 always (cheap); ready(): 200 iff deps ok
// K8s: unready stops traffic, live failure restarts

quiz.explain: Separating them avoids restart loops during outages.
options: Liveness gates traffic; readiness gates restarts
Readiness gates traffic; liveness gates restarts
Both should fail when the database is down
They are the same check, just run on two ports
quiz.q: Readiness versus liveness in Kubernetes?

takeaway: Gate traffic with readiness and reserve liveness for true deadlocks.
trap: Failing liveness on downstream slowness and restart-looping.

body_md: Blue-green runs two full stacks and flips traffic once green passes checks. It gives instant rollback and full isolation at double cost plus migration care for state.
hook: Blue-green deploys: two stacks, one flip, instant rollback.

quiz.explain: A full parallel stack makes cutover and rollback one traffic flip; the shared database still needs compatible schemas.
options: When you want to test on 1% of traffic first
When you cannot afford to run double capacity
When you need an instant, atomic rollback path
When schema changes can't be backward compatible
quiz.q: When is blue-green worth the cost?

takeaway: Keep parallel stacks for atomic cutover and instant rollback.
trap: Forgetting state migration while flipping stateless traffic.

body_md: Canary shifts a slice of traffic to the new build and watches error and latency deltas. Automate promotion and rollback on burn signals instead of eyeballing dashboards.
code:
// 1% -> 10% -> 50% with auto rollback
if error_delta > limit { rollback(); }
hook: Canary releases: let 1% bleed before 100% do.
output:
1% -> 10% -> 50% while deltas stay green
error_delta > limit -> rollback() at once

quiz.explain: Gradual exposure with auto rollback limits blast radius.
options: Deploy to all hosts, hidden behind a feature flag
Run the new build in staging for a full week
Replace every host at once to minimize drift
Expose a small slice; promote if metrics hold
quiz.q: How does canary reduce release risk?

takeaway: Shift traffic gradually with automatic rollback on metric regression.
trap: Canarying without rollback automation during a metric spike.

body_md: Feature flags decouple deploy from release with targeted rollouts. Flag by user cohort, keep flags short-lived, and always ship a kill switch for risky paths.
hook: Feature flags: ship code dark, light it up by cohort.
output:
cohort in -> rank_v2; rest -> rank_v1
// kill switch flips everyone back instantly

quiz.explain: Cohort targeting plus expiry keeps flags safe and clean.
options: Keep every flag forever in case you need it
Wrap every code path in its own permanent flag
Short-lived flags, cohort rollout, kill switch
Flip flags for all users at once on release
quiz.q: Healthy feature flag practice?

takeaway: Roll out by cohort with short-lived flags and kill switches.
trap: Leaving stale flags that fork logic forever.

body_md: RED tracks rate errors duration per service while USE tracks utilization saturation errors per resource. RED spots user pain fast and USE finds the bottlenecked disk or queue beneath.
hook: RED feels user pain, USE finds the cause.

quiz.explain: Service signals plus resource signals connect symptoms to causes.
options: RED for resources, USE for services
RED for logs, USE for tracing spans
RED for services, USE for resources
RED for alerts, USE for capacity only
quiz.q: How do RED and USE metrics split the work?

takeaway: Pair service signals with resource signals to link pain to cause.
trap: Alerting on CPU alone while errors climb unnoticed.

body_md: Tracing samples to keep cost sane while catching tails. Head-sample errors and slow paths, tail-sample interesting traces, and propagate baggage so spans join across services.
code:
// sample slow or error traces, keep 1% baseline
if latency > slo || err { keep(); }
hook: Trace sampling: sample smart so slow tails cannot hide.
output:
slow/error traces kept; 1% baseline kept
// tails stay visible; storage stays bounded

quiz.explain: Adaptive sampling keeps signal while bounding storage cost.
options: A fixed 0.1% head sample of every request
Record 100% of traces and just compress them
Sample only successful requests to cut noise
Keep errors and slow traces, sample the rest
quiz.q: How do you sample traces at scale?

takeaway: Sample adaptively to keep errors and slow paths without excess cost.
trap: Sampling uniformly and losing every rare tail event.

body_md: Burn-rate alerts fire on how fast you eat error budget. Page on fast burn over short windows and ticket on slow burn over days so noise drops but real outages still wake someone.
code:
// fast: 14x burn over 1h -> page
// slow: 1x burn over 3d -> ticket
hook: Alert on budget burn, not on every spike.
output:
fast burn (14x/1h) -> page; slow burn (1x/3d) -> ticket
// budget-aware; short spikes alone stay quiet

quiz.explain: Dual windows separate urgent outages from slow leaks.
options: Page on fast burn, ticket on slow burn
Page on every error spike above one percent
Alert only once the budget is fully spent
Average errors over 30 days, then page
quiz.q: How do burn-rate alerts cut noise?

takeaway: Page on fast budget burn and ticket slow leaks separately.
trap: Paging on every short spike without budget context.
